metadata.title: Ten Questions for Mathematics Teachers… and how PISA can help answer them

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This OECD report synthesizes findings from PISA 2012 (student and school background questionnaires plus mathematics assessment results) and TALIS 2013 (teacher questionnaire). The excerpt provided does not specify whether analysts applied PISA/TALIS sampling weights or replicate-weight procedures, nor does it name any weight variables. Because the report is a teacher guide that summarizes descriptive and correlational patterns rather than presenting a fully specified ML estimation pipeline, the weighting strategy is not documented in the provided text. For any re-analysis using PISA/TALIS microdata, analysts should apply the complex survey design weights supplied by OECD/IEA and use the corresponding replicate weights (if provided) to obtain correct standard errors.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The report is a teacher guide that summarizes relationships between reported teaching/learning strategies and mathematics performance, but the provided text does not describe an explicit PV-based achievement modeling procedure (e.g., how PISA plausible values were combined) or any missing-data handling method. Since the excerpt does not specify the dependent variable as a PV-based cognitive score within a documented estimation framework, PV handling cannot be classified from the text. This is therefore a reporting gap for PV and missing-data procedures rather than evidence that PVs are genuinely not used.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used PISA 2012 mathematics assessment data for 15-year-old students and their background questionnaire responses, and TALIS 2013 teacher questionnaire data for lower secondary teachers. The excerpt does not specify additional analytic restrictions (e.g., grade bands, school types, or exclusions) beyond the standard PISA/TALIS target populations.

data.outcome_summary: This OECD teacher guide uses cross-sectional PISA 2012 mathematics results (for 15-year-old students) together with student background questionnaire responses about mathematics class experiences and teaching practices, and it also incorporates TALIS 2013 teacher questionnaire data on teaching practices and teacher self-efficacy. The report organizes evidence into ten classroom-focused questions, including how teacher-directed versus student-oriented strategies relate to students’ success across mathematics item difficulty, and how strategy use varies by student gender and socio-economic status. It emphasizes that PISA and TALIS are collected at one point in time and therefore cannot establish cause-and-effect relationships. The excerpt does not provide a technical ML modeling specification (algorithms, validation metrics, or PV/missing-data procedures), so the findings are presented as descriptive/correlational patterns and evidence-informed recommendations for teachers rather than as model-based predictive performance.
data.null_fields_interpretation: The provided text is a non-technical teacher guide that describes the data sources (PISA 2012 and TALIS 2013) and summarizes patterns, but it does not report an empirical ML pipeline with a defined target variable, algorithms, or performance metrics. It also does not provide sample sizes, per-country Ns, or explicit PV and missing-data handling procedures in the excerpt. Therefore, several quantitative extraction fields (countries, total_students, ML techniques, and structured predictive findings) cannot be populated from the supplied content.
